events.title: Day two on Route 66, somewhere past Amarillo. The truck has overheated and you've pulled to the shoulder to let the engine cool.
events.text: A woman is standing in the dust ahead with two small children and a cardboard case. Her husband is not there — she doesn't say where he is. She has no vehicle. She asks if there is room. Your truck is already carrying your wife, your mother, your teenage son, and everything you own in the world. There is water in a jug under the seat. Your son is watching you. Your wife is watching you. The woman's children are watching the ground.

choices.text: Tell her you're sorry, that you can't take on more weight, and pull back onto the road.
choices.result: You have decided that the family you were given is the family you can afford to keep. The road did not make you hard — it made the cost of softness visible, and you chose to see it clearly.

choices.text: Tell her to put her children in the truck bed and climb up herself.
choices.result: You have decided that the line around your family was drawn in the wrong place, or that you cannot live with yourself if you drive away. You do not know yet what this will cost. You have made it someone else's problem too, and your own problem larger.

events.title: Dust Still in the Air
events.text: You pull into a roadside camp outside Shamrock. A dozen families are here, all Oklahoma or Texas, all telling the same story — the topsoil just blew away. An older man says the land was ruined by years of dry-farming wheat with no cover crops left on the fields.
trivia: Dust storms in the 1930s reached the East Coast, darkening skies as far as Washington D.C.
The Dust Bowl affected 100 million acres across the Southern Plains.

choices.text: Stay the night and share what you know about the road ahead.
choices.result: You sit up late trading information. Your wife counts the beans you shared and says nothing.

choices.text: Rest the family, keep to yourselves, move on at dawn.
choices.result: The family sleeps well. You don't learn much, and the others notice you didn't offer.

choices.text: Ask where the relief stations are and leave before dark.
choices.result: You get the information and drive on. Nobody helped you and you helped nobody.

events.title: The Arizona Line
events.text: A state trooper waves you to the shoulder at the Arizona border. He says there's a 'processing fee' for Okies coming through — it's not a real law, just a shakedown. He eyes the truck bed and your mother in the back seat.
trivia: California and other western states set up 'bum blockades' to turn back destitute migrants.
The 1937 Indigent Act in California attempted to bar poor migrants from entering the state.

choices.text: Pay the two dollars and keep moving.
choices.result: Two dollars gone. The family moves safely. It burns, but you're through.

choices.text: Argue. You know this isn't legal.

outcomes.result: He makes you wait two hours in the sun then takes the money anyway. The kids are exhausted.
He lets you through. Your son watched and stood a little straighter.

choices.text: Turn around. Find a back road.
choices.result: The back road costs a half day and a tank of gas. Your mother asks how much longer.

image.artist: Matthew Anderson (based on an original .JPG format picture found at the AARoads shield gallery.)

events.title: Church Hall in Needles
events.text: A small Baptist church is handing out food boxes on the highway shoulder. There's enough for maybe thirty families and you count forty trucks. A young mother near the back of the line looks like she hasn't slept in two days.
trivia: Church groups and the Red Cross operated relief stations along Route 66 throughout the 1930s migration.

choices.text: Take your share and keep the line moving.
choices.result: Beans, cornmeal, a can of peaches. The kids eat well tonight.

choices.text: Wave off your box — let the woman behind you take it.
choices.result: She thanks you. Your daughter asks why you didn't take the food. You don't have a quick answer.

choices.text: Take two boxes while the crowd is distracted.
choices.result: Nobody stops you. Somebody at the end of the line gets nothing. You know it.

events.title: Radiator Steam, Mojave Desert
events.text: The truck shudders and a geyser of steam erupts from the hood. You're on a flat stretch of the Mojave with no shade and maybe a pint of water left. A man in a newer truck slows down and offers to sell you a spare hose for three dollars.

choices.text: Pay the three dollars for the hose.
choices.result: An hour of work under the hood and you're moving again. Worth every cent.

choices.text: Haggle him down to a dollar fifty.

outcomes.result: He takes it. You shake hands and get rolling before noon.
He drives on. You wait four hours in the heat until another family stops. It costs you more in the end.

choices.text: Try to patch it with rags and tape.

outcomes.result: It holds for thirty miles then blows again. You lose most of the afternoon.
Your son holds the rag tight while you tape it. It holds. Small wins feel large out here.

image.artist: Ken Lund from Reno, Nevada, USA

events.title: Weedpatch Camp — A Different Kind of Place
events.text: You pull into Arvin Federal Camp. It has flush toilets, showers, and a school. The manager, Tom Collins, meets you at the gate. He says there are rules here — families govern themselves — and there's room if you want it. The private grower's camp down the road is cheaper but there are no sanitation facilities.
trivia: Tom Collins ran the Arvin Federal Camp and kept detailed journals that Steinbeck used in writing The Grapes of Wrath.
Federal migrant camps provided sanitation, medical care, and self-governance rare in private grower camps.

choices.text: Stay at Weedpatch. Pay the small fee.
choices.result: The children wash for the first time in two weeks. Your mother sits in a real chair. Something loosens in all of you.

choices.text: Take the cheaper private camp to save cash.
choices.result: You save the fee. The ditch running past the tents smells bad. Your youngest coughs all night.

events.title: The Contractor's Terms
events.text: A labor contractor at the edge of a peach orchard offers the family work — fifteen cents a box, twelve hours a day, housing in the grower's camp included. The rate is half what he advertised on the handbills that brought you here. You're nearly out of money. Other families are waiting behind you for the same offer.

choices.text: Take the work. Feed the family first.
choices.result: You sign. The family eats. The families behind you see you accept the rate and the contractor stops negotiating with everyone.

choices.text: Refuse and tell the others the rate is cheating them.
choices.result: Three families walk away with you. The contractor holds the line two days then raises the rate. Your wife counts the beans you have left.

choices.text: Accept quietly and say nothing to the others.
choices.result: You eat. You keep your head down. The road ends here, and it cost you something you can't name.

events.title: A week later, in a camp outside Barstow. A family two tents over is short on food and the father comes to ask if you can spare anything. Your own supplies are low.

text.default: You've kept the circle tight this whole road, and it has held. Your children have not gone hungry. You look at the man and you recognize him completely — he is you, two days earlier, before you made your choice. You tell him you don't have enough to spare. It is probably true. You go back inside the tent and your son doesn't say anything, and neither do you.

variants.text: You've kept the circle tight this whole road, and it has held. Your children have not gone hungry. You look at the man and you recognize him completely — he is you, two days earlier, before you made your choice. You tell him you don't have enough to spare. It is probably true. You go back inside the tent and your son doesn't say anything, and neither do you.

The woman you carried out of Texas is in the camp with you — her and her children have become a fact of your days, like weather. When the man from two tents over comes asking, she is the one who answers before you do, offering what little she has. You watch your son watch her do it. You don't know if you've built something or just made the disaster bigger and more crowded. You give what you can.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Hugh Hammond Bennett
sages.title: Chief of the Soil Conservation Service
sages.bio: Hugh Hammond Bennett spent decades warning that deep plowing and removal of native grasses was destroying the Southern Plains. When the Dust Bowl proved him right, Roosevelt appointed him to lead the new Soil Conservation Service in 1935.
sages.greeting: A government truck is parked at the roadside, and a sunburned man in a USDA jacket is studying the cracked earth along the shoulder. He introduces himself as Hugh Bennett.
sages.advice: "The grass held this soil for ten thousand years. We plowed it all up in twenty." He shows you a photograph of a field — topsoil gone, hardpan exposed. "What you're driving away from didn't just happen. It was built, one bad season at a time."

question.question: What farming practice most directly caused the Dust Bowl's massive soil erosion?
choices: Planting too many fruit orchards instead of wheat
Removing native grasses and deep-plowing fragile prairie soil for wheat farms
Using too much irrigation water which loosened the topsoil
Railroad construction that tore up the land across the Plains
question.explanation: Native grasses had deep root systems that held the Plains topsoil in place for millennia. When farmers plowed them under for wheat fields and drought hit, there were no roots to anchor the soil — it simply blew away in massive dust storms.
question.teksRef: 8.29(C) — Environmental and economic causes of the Dust Bowl and westward migration

sages.name: Dorothea Lange
sages.title: Farm Security Administration Photographer
sages.bio: Dorothea Lange photographed migrant workers across California for the Farm Security Administration beginning in 1935. Her image 'Migrant Mother,' taken at a pea-pickers' camp in 1936, became the defining image of the Depression and prompted emergency federal food aid.
sages.greeting: A woman with a large camera is crouched near a family's tent at the roadside camp. She stands as you walk over. Her name is Dorothea Lange, and she works for the government — not the kind that turns you away.
sages.advice: "I want to photograph your family, if you'll allow it. Not to shame you — to show people what this actually looks like." She pauses. "People in Washington are making decisions about your life without ever seeing your face."

question.question: Why did the Farm Security Administration send photographers like Dorothea Lange to document migrants?
choices: To create wanted posters for migrants who crossed state lines illegally
To build public and political support for New Deal relief programs
To sell photographs to newspapers for profit
To count how many families had left Oklahoma for official census records
question.explanation: The FSA's photography program was designed to make the human cost of the Depression visible to the American public and to Congress. Lange's images of migrant families — especially 'Migrant Mother' — created political pressure that translated directly into emergency relief funding.
question.teksRef: 8.29(D) — Role of New Deal programs and media in responding to the Great Depression

sages.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: Franklin Roosevelt took office in 1933 and launched the New Deal — a series of programs designed to provide relief, recovery, and reform. For tenant farmers and migrants, the New Deal's Farm Security Administration created federal migrant camps, resettlement loans, and photographic documentation of the crisis.
sages.greeting: A campaign poster on the wall of a diner shows Roosevelt's face. The owner turns up the radio — Roosevelt is giving a fireside chat. You sit down with your coffee and listen.
sages.advice: Roosevelt's voice fills the room: "The test of our progress is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little." The diner owner says he's heard it three times and it still sounds true.

question.question: Which New Deal agency built and operated the federal migrant camps that gave Dust Bowl families access to sanitation and self-governance?
choices: The Civilian Conservation Corps
The Farm Security Administration
The Tennessee Valley Authority
The Social Security Administration
question.explanation: The Farm Security Administration, created in 1937 from the earlier Resettlement Administration, built and operated the federal migrant labor camps in California. These camps — including the one at Arvin run by Tom Collins — provided sanitation, medical care, and democratic self-governance to migrant families.
question.teksRef: 8.29(D) — New Deal programs addressing tenant farmer displacement and migration

eventTrivia.question: What was the main cause of topsoil loss during the Dust Bowl?
choices: Flooding rivers
Removal of native grasses through plowing
Overuse of irrigation
Railroad construction
eventTrivia.fact: Native grasses held Plains soil in place. When farmers plowed them under, drought-dried soil had nothing anchoring it and blew away.

eventTrivia.question: Which states were most severely hit by the Dust Bowl?
choices: New England and the Midwest
The Southern Plains — Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Colorado
The Pacific Northwest and California
The Deep South — Mississippi and Alabama
eventTrivia.fact: The Dust Bowl's epicenter was the Southern Plains, especially the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southern Kansas, and eastern Colorado.

eventTrivia.question: What was the main highway Dust Bowl migrants used to travel west to California?
choices: Highway 1
Route 66
The Lincoln Highway
The Santa Fe Trail
eventTrivia.fact: Route 66, running from Oklahoma City to Los Angeles, was the primary route for Dust Bowl migrants heading west — they called it 'The Mother Road.'

eventTrivia.question: What nickname did Californians give to Dust Bowl migrants from Oklahoma?
choices: Exodusters
Boomers
Okies
Sooners
eventTrivia.fact: 'Okies' became the derogatory term for all Dust Bowl migrants, regardless of which state they actually came from.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Farm Security Administration do for migrant families in California?
choices: Provided free land grants in the Central Valley
Built and ran federal camps with sanitation and self-governance
Paid farmers to return to Oklahoma
Organized migrant unions to negotiate wages
eventTrivia.fact: The FSA built federal migrant camps — like Arvin (Weedpatch) — that offered flush toilets, showers, medical care, and elected camp councils, unlike filthy private grower camps.

eventTrivia.question: Why did California try to turn back Dust Bowl migrants at its borders?
choices: Migrants carried a disease California feared would spread
State officials feared economic strain from thousands of destitute arrivals
Federal law required California to screen migrants
Migrants were suspected of communist organizing
eventTrivia.fact: California feared the economic burden of hundreds of thousands of destitute migrants. Some counties and the LAPD ran 'bum blockades' at state lines, though the legal basis was shaky.

eventTrivia.question: What was a tenant farmer's relationship to the land they worked?
choices: They owned the land outright but owed taxes to the county
They farmed land owned by someone else, paying rent in crops or cash
They were paid wages by the government to maintain federal farmland
They leased land from Native American tribes under treaty agreements
eventTrivia.fact: Tenant farmers and sharecroppers worked land owned by landlords, paying rent as a share of their crop. When crops failed and debt mounted, landlords could foreclose and evict.

eventTrivia.question: What role did mechanization play in displacing tenant farmers?
choices: New tractors required more workers to operate them
One tractor could do the work of many tenant families, making their labor unnecessary
Machines broke down so often that farmers relied more on human labor
The government banned mechanization to protect sharecropper jobs
eventTrivia.fact: A single tractor could plow land that previously required dozens of tenant families. Landlords increasingly mechanized and evicted tenants whose labor was no longer needed.

eventTrivia.question: What did Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' prompt the federal government to do?
choices: Pass a law banning migration between states
Send emergency food supplies to a California migrant camp
Create Route 66 as an official federal highway
Draft men from migrant camps into the Civilian Conservation Corps
eventTrivia.fact: After 'Migrant Mother' was published in 1936, the federal government rushed emergency food relief — 20,000 pounds of food — to the pea-pickers' camp at Nipomo, California.

eventTrivia.question: What was the average wage offered to migrant farm workers in California's Central Valley in the late 1930s?
choices: A fair union wage negotiated by the AFL
Wages set deliberately low because migrants' desperation gave growers all the leverage
Government-mandated minimum wage equal to local workers
Higher wages than local workers because migrants had specialized skills
eventTrivia.fact: The flood of desperate migrants gave California growers enormous leverage. Wages were driven down precisely because so many families needed work and had nowhere else to go.

eventTrivia.question: How many people are estimated to have migrated out of the Dust Bowl states during the 1930s?
choices: About 10,000
About 100,000
About 3.5 million
About 20 million
eventTrivia.fact: Roughly 3.5 million people left the Southern Plains during the 1930s — one of the largest internal migrations in American history.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Soil Conservation Service created to do?
choices: Provide cash loans to displaced tenant farmers
Teach farmers erosion-prevention techniques and restore grasslands
Build irrigation systems across the Great Plains
Buy land from bankrupt farmers and redistribute it
eventTrivia.fact: Hugh Hammond Bennett's Soil Conservation Service, established in 1935, trained farmers in contour plowing, crop rotation, and windbreaks — practices designed to stop the erosion that caused the Dust Bowl.

eventTrivia.question: What was a 'Hooverville'?
choices: A government-built housing project named after President Hoover
A makeshift shantytown built by unemployed and homeless Americans during the Depression
A nickname for the new CCC camps in national forests
A tent city set up by the Army for veterans of World War I
eventTrivia.fact: Hoovervilles were shantytowns of cardboard, wood scraps, and tin that unemployed Americans built on the edges of cities during the Depression — sarcastically named after President Herbert Hoover, blamed for the crisis.

eventTrivia.question: What was the primary reason banks foreclosed on tenant farmers during the 1930s?
choices: Farmers refused to pay taxes on their land
Drought destroyed crops, eliminating income needed to pay rent and loans
The government ordered banks to consolidate small farms into large ones
Farmers abandoned fields voluntarily to seek better land in the West
eventTrivia.fact: Years of drought meant no crops, which meant no income, which meant farmers could not pay debts or rent. Banks and landlords foreclosed, stripping families of the only livelihood they had.

eventTrivia.question: What was Tom Collins's job at the Arvin Federal Camp?
choices: He was a labor contractor recruiting migrants for growers
He was the camp manager who kept detailed records Steinbeck later used
He was an FSA photographer documenting migrant conditions
He was a USDA soil scientist studying erosion at the camp
eventTrivia.fact: Tom Collins managed the Arvin (Weedpatch) federal camp and kept meticulous journals about camp life. John Steinbeck visited, read Collins's notes, and drew on them directly when writing The Grapes of Wrath.

eventTrivia.question: Why were large numbers of Dust Bowl migrants NOT welcomed by California communities?
choices: Most migrants were wanted by law enforcement in their home states
Locals feared competition for scarce jobs and resented the economic burden
California had a treaty with Oklahoma banning labor migration
Migrants brought crops that competed with California's farms
eventTrivia.fact: The Depression had already strained California's economy. Local residents and officials feared that hundreds of thousands of destitute newcomers would take jobs, depress wages, and overwhelm relief systems.

data.historicalContext: Between 1930 and 1940, roughly 3.5 million people left the Southern Plains states due to drought, debt, and mechanization. Most traveled Route 66 to California, where they found not the promised land but a hostile labor market, discriminatory roadblocks, and wages deliberately kept low by growers who understood that desperation is leverage. The federal migrant camp system — run by the Farm Security Administration — provided islands of dignity amid the hostility, but it served only a fraction of those who needed it. The Dust Bowl generation's migration reshaped California demographically, strained the New Deal politically, and left a lasting imprint on American culture through the photographs of Dorothea Lange and the fiction of John Steinbeck.

verdict.good: You drove this road like a man who knew the people around him were real. When the water jug was full you thought about who else was thirsty. When the contractor offered you a way out, you looked back at the families behind you before you decided. It cost you — cash, sleep, maybe a fight with your wife about beans. The strike broke inside a week and the contractor raised the rate two cents. Two cents. That was the whole fight. It doesn't sound like much. It was everything.
verdict.bad: You kept the family fed and the truck running and you told yourself that was enough. Every time the choice came down to yours or theirs, you chose yours — the food box, the contractor's offer, the quick road out. You weren't a cruel man. Cruelty takes commitment. You just looked away, every time, when looking away was easier. You made it to California. A lot of the people you passed on the road made it too, with less than you had when you started, because you had it and didn't share it. You arrived. So did they. You'll never know what it cost them.
verdict.indifferent: You drove Route 66 and arrived. The truck held. The family made it. You took the safe choice every time one appeared, not because it was right but because it was there. The Dust Bowl was the largest internal migration in American history. Three and a half million people on the same road, the same desperation, the same question about what a person owes a stranger. You passed through it without ever really answering. History will record the ones who stood for something. You were present. That's what can be said.

data.reviewSummary:
The Dust Bowl was born from choices made long before the storms arrived. For decades, farmers across the Southern Plains plowed under native grasses to plant wheat, removing the deep root systems that held the fragile prairie soil in place. When drought hit in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil turned to dust and blew away in walls of darkness that reached as far as Washington, D.C. The Dust Bowl's worst damage fell on the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southern Kansas, and eastern Colorado — the Southern Plains heartland.

Tenant farmers and sharecroppers — people who worked land they didn't own, paying rent as a share of their crops — had no cushion when the harvests failed. Debt mounted, landlords foreclosed, and mechanization accelerated the crisis: one tractor could now do the work of many tenant families, making their labor unnecessary. Roughly 3.5 million people left the Plains during the 1930s, most of them following Route 66 west toward California — a road migrants called 'The Mother Road.'

California was not waiting with open arms. State officials and local residents feared the economic strain of so many destitute arrivals. Counties organized roadblocks, and migrants — called 'Okies' regardless of which state they came from — found wages in the Central Valley deliberately kept low because growers understood that desperation is leverage.

The federal government responded through the Farm Security Administration, which built migrant camps offering flush toilets, showers, medical care, and self-governing camp councils. The Arvin Federal Camp at Weedpatch, managed by Tom Collins, was one of these islands of dignity. Collins kept detailed journals about camp life that John Steinbeck later drew on when writing The Grapes of Wrath.

Hugh Hammond Bennett, leading the Soil Conservation Service created in 1935, taught farmers contour plowing and windbreak planting to stop the erosion. Dorothea Lange photographed migrant families for the FSA; her 1936 image 'Migrant Mother' prompted the federal government to rush emergency food relief to a California camp. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal, particularly the Farm Security Administration, was the primary federal response to the displacement of tenant farmers.

data.title: CORPS OF DISCOVERY
data.subtitle: St. Louis to the Pacific, 1804–1806
data.introBody: Spring, 1804. St. Louis, Missouri. President Jefferson has tasked you to lead the Corps of Discovery into unknown territory — to map the Louisiana Purchase, find a route to the Pacific, and report what you find. Choose your supplies carefully. The wilderness does not forgive poor planning.
data.trailFeedOpener: May 1804: the Corps pushes off from Camp Dubois into the Missouri River current.

events.title: The Mandan Villages
events.text: You reach the Mandan villages near present-day North Dakota. The Mandans are skilled traders who know the land ahead. How you treat them will shape the rest of the expedition.
trivia: The Mandans were expert farmers and traders who had dealt with many peoples before Lewis and Clark arrived.

sageAdvice.name: Sacagawea
sageAdvice.line: Gifts and respect open doors that force cannot.

choices.text: Trade fairly. Share goods and learn their maps.
choices.result: The Mandans share detailed geographic knowledge. You winter here and emerge stronger.

choices.text: Take what you need. Keep moving.
choices.result: You press on, but word travels fast. Future tribes will be wary.

choices.text: Camp nearby but keep distance.
choices.result: A cautious winter. You miss vital geographic knowledge but avoid conflict.

events.title: The Great Falls Portage
events.text: The Great Falls of the Missouri block your path. You must haul canoes and gear overland 18 miles around the falls — a brutal task that takes weeks in summer heat.
trivia: The Great Falls portage was one of the most physically demanding stretches of the entire expedition.

choices.text: Split the work. Rotate crews daily.
choices.result: Slow but steady. The rotation keeps men from breaking down entirely.

choices.text: Push everyone hard. Finish fast.
choices.result: You finish the portage quickly, but three men suffer serious injuries that linger.

choices.text: Cache heavy gear. Travel light.

outcomes.result: Smart call. You move faster and the cached goods are waiting on the return.
Animals raid the cache. You lose field notes and some provisions.

events.title: Crossing the Rockies
events.text: The Rocky Mountains loom ahead. You cannot cross without horses, and only the Shoshone have them. Sacagawea recognizes the chief — her brother. Everything depends on this moment.
trivia: Sacagawea's reunion with her Shoshone brother Cameahwait was a turning point that secured the horses needed to cross the Rockies.

choices.text: Let Sacagawea lead the talks. Trust her.
choices.result: Cameahwait provides horses and a guide. The Rockies are hard but passable.

choices.text: Negotiate firmly. Offer trade goods first.

sages.bio: Sacagawea was a Shoshone woman who joined the expedition at Fort Mandan with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau. Her knowledge of terrain, languages, and Native peoples proved essential — and her presence signaled the Corps came in peace.

sages.advice: "The tribes ahead judge you by how you treated the ones behind. Bring gifts and patience. Leave demands at camp."

sages.name: William Clark
sages.title: Co-Commander, Corps of Discovery
sages.bio: William Clark served as co-commander and the expedition's primary mapmaker. His meticulous charts of the Missouri River and Columbia watershed gave the United States its first accurate picture of the western interior.
sages.greeting: Clark spreads a new chart on a flat rock near the Columbia River. He marks the coast with a careful line.
sages.advice: "Every river, every portage, every tribe — I write it all down. Future Americans will follow these marks. Make sure what we leave behind is true."

question.question: What was one major result of the Lewis and Clark Expedition for the United States?

data.historicalContext: The Corps of Discovery departed in May 1804 and reached the Pacific in November 1805, returning to St. Louis in September 1806. Lewis and Clark produced the first accurate maps of the western interior and documented over 300 species new to science. Their interactions with more than 50 Native nations were sometimes respectful and sometimes marked by the power imbalance of American expansion. The expedition directly opened the door to the Oregon Trail era and the massive westward migration that followed — displacing the very peoples Lewis and Clark had recorded.

verdict.good: You led with respect and recorded the truth. When the Mandan offered knowledge you took it with gratitude; when Sacagawea led you followed. The Corps reached the Pacific and came home. History will record what you saw — and also what came after: the settlers who used your maps never asked the peoples you met whether they wanted to be found. You served Jefferson's mission faithfully. Whether that mission was just is a harder question, and you are old enough to ask it.
verdict.bad: You took what you needed and moved on. The tribes fed you, guided you, and watched you pass through their land as though it were yours already — because that was always the plan, and you knew it, and it suited you. You reached the Pacific. The expedition is a success in the ledgers. But the goodwill you burned was real, the insults you delivered were remembered, and the nations you dismissed were the ones your maps would be used against. You did the job. You did not do it well.
verdict.indifferent: You drifted through the continent and came out the other side. Not cruel, not particularly kind — just present. The decisions that shaped the expedition got made by the current, by circumstance, by whoever pushed hardest in the moment. You were there when Sacagawea found her brother and got the horses. You were there when the Corps reached the Pacific. You took notes. The expedition happened around you more than because of you. History recorded the journey. It had less to say about the ones who simply went along for the ride.

data.reviewSummary:
In May 1804, President Thomas Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark west to explore the Louisiana Territory, which the United States had purchased from France in 1803. Jefferson's instructions were clear: map the land, find a navigable route to the Pacific Ocean, and document the peoples, animals, and plants encountered along the way.

The Corps of Discovery numbered about 33 people and traveled up the Missouri River through present-day Kansas, Nebraska, and the Dakotas. They wintered at Fort Mandan, where they met Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman married to the French-Canadian trader Toussaint Charbonneau. Sacagawea joined the expedition as an interpreter and guide. Her presence with an infant signaled to Native nations that the Corps was not a war party — making peaceful trade and passage possible. When the Corps reached the Rocky Mountains, it was Sacagawea who recognized her own brother, Chief Cameahwait of the Shoshone, and secured the horses the expedition needed to cross the mountains.

The Great Falls of the Missouri required an eighteen-mile overland portage — one of the hardest stretches of the journey. Beyond the Rockies the Corps descended the Columbia River, running dangerous rapids past Chinook villages, and reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805. They built Fort Clatsop on the Oregon coast and wintered there before returning to St. Louis in September 1806.

The expedition produced the first accurate maps of the western interior and documented more than 300 species new to science. Lewis and Clark met over fifty Native nations; interactions ranged from respectful exchange to tense confrontation. Back home, their journals and charts opened the door to westward expansion — inspiring the waves of settlers, missionaries, and traders who followed the same routes in the decades ahead, fundamentally and permanently changing the lives of the Native peoples the Corps had recorded.
